Damplaas Kragbron

By: Eugene Botha | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
........a 40 year old power generation success story is now jeopardized by politicians

Unique Selling Point:
The story is about a group of farmers who have created 320 km of power distribution infrastrcuture and have been running it successfully for 40 years. It is a prime example of how private initiatives can alleviate electricity problems. The otehr side of the story is the fact that SALGA says only municipalities are allowed to distribute power and want to confiscate this marvellous initiatve and hand it over to a defunct and bankrupt local municipality to run.

Summary:
The story is about a group of farmers who have created 320 km of power distribution infrastrcuture and have been running it successfully for 40 years. It is a prime example of how private initiatives can alleviate electricity problems. The otehr side of the story is the fact that SALGA says only municipalities are allowed to distribute power and want to confiscate this marvellous initiatve and hand it over to a defunct and bankrupt local municipality to run.

Further information:
Damplaas Kragbron
In a time where South Africa’s energy supply is in serious trouble, with rolling blackouts and near unaffordable power tariffs, new solutions are needed. And there is an example of a private solution that has been working exceptionally well for 30 years – but it is now also under serious threat.

Damplaas Kragbron has been supplying reliable and affordable electricity to their community for more than 30 years. They have 320 km of power lines and has 175 transformers and supply power to the districts of Heilron, Lindely, Bethlehem and Reitz. It is situated in the Freestate town of Petrus Steyn. It has been highly successful and is well maintained.

They buy electricity in bulk from Eskom and distribute it via their network with a small additional fee added. It all started 40 years ago when Eskom was not yet supplying power in the area. The farmers stood together and decided to establish their own network to get electricity to the various farms in the various districts and over the years it has grown to a network spanning 320 km.

The network is crucial to the many irrigation farmers, chicken farms and other users such as a fertilizer factory and maize silos. The network supplies power to these enities and farmer who would not otherwise have had access to power. And their tariffs are 13% cheaper than Eskom’s rural tariffs and 20% cheaper than the local Neketoane municipality in Reitz. The whole network is currently valued at more than R50 million and was built with private money.

They also have an additional 25 transformers which Eskom continuously want to borrow. They maintain the infrastructure and when Eskom customers lose power, they are still online.

Truly a success story!!

But that is not the end of it. Last week they were served with papers in which SALGA demands that the network be transferred to the dysfunctional and bankrupt local municipality.

SALGA’s argument is that only municipalities are allowed to distribute electricity.

Damplaas is opposing this, because if this is allowed to happen not only will tariffs skyrocket when the municipality takes over, the municipality does not have the capacity or knowledge to maintain the network. It all spells disaster for something that is working so well, and it will jeopardise farming operations in numerous districts, with severe job losses.

Instead of trying to bring a perfectly functioning project into a failing system, why not learn from it and rather duplicate it in other places, the farmers ask.

Interviewees:
Jan Snyman -- MD of Damplaas Kragbron
Thabu Bosman -- Damplaas lawyer and potato farmer
SALGA
TK Pooe, Wits School of Governance

Case studies:
• Johan Claassen who has 42 000 chickens and for whom power is crucial
• Jannie Wepner an irrigation farmer, farming with maize. Totally reliant on electricity for irrigation.

The story was discussed with John Webb and Anna Maria and John's comments were:

From: John Webb
Sent: Tuesday, 02 November 2021 2:55 PM
To: Eugene Botha ; Anna-Maria van Niekerk
Subject: RE: Proposal in place of "My Voice" -- Eugene

Hi Eugene,

Certainly sounds like a story to me if we can really personalise the narrative. If we could get a sense of the frustration at being forced to hand over this functioning system. I think we need to spend time in some of these places, see the people working and living there – get a slice of their daily lives – then introduce the idea of mismanagement’s dark cloud looming over the horizon. Could be very nice.

J

Script:


V/O:
On the farm Arras in the Eastern Free State Jannie Wepner and his son Phillip carefully maintain the electricity supply to a pump station on one of their dams. It’s key for the irrigation system feeding their crops throughout the year, dodging the impacts what can be erratic rainfall in the part of the country. This constant supply of pumped water has given them bumper crops year after year.
Derek:
Jannie, how long have you been farming in this area?

Jannie:
Ek is nou die derde generasie, my seun Philip is die 4e generasie en sy klein seuntjie,, hy is die 5e generasie.
V/O:
And for the past 40 years this family has been planting wheat on a large scale only because they have access to reliable electricity to run their pumps. Without the pumps their crops would wither and die.
V/O:
The Wepners, like more than a hundred and seventy other farmers in the area, have access to power through a private electricity distribution network called Damplaas Kragbron, situated in the town of Petrus Steyn.

The Damplaas network also supplies power to a large fertilizer plant and a chicken farm where more than eight hundred thousand chickens are raised.

The farms and industries using the network in turn provide jobs for thousands of people in the area. For forty years, the system has been at the centre of the region’s development.
LINK:
And then like a lightning bolt out of the blue, on the 21st of October last year Damplaas was served with high court papers by the South African Local Government Organization, SALGA, which is challenging the legitimacy of their operation.
V/O:
SALGA is an umbrella organization meant to assist municipalities in various ways.

Thabu Bosman is a potato farmer and an attorney acting for Damplaas. Like other beneficiaries, Bosman worries SALGA’s court challenge will derail four decades of sucess.
Derek:
Give us a synopsis Thabo, what are they saying?

Thabu:
They want to take our existing rights away. They say that municipalities have the exclusive authority to reticulate electricity within their jurisdictions.
V/O:
SALGA is in effect asking the court to rule that no other entities, other than municipalities, be allowed to distribute electricity.

If it succeeds, it’ll spell the end of Damplaas. The local Nketoana municipality that currently distributes power only in the town, will have to start supplying electricity to farms as well.

And here, the omens are not good. On our arrival in Petrus Steyn, we stopped in the town centre and were struck by the neglect: infrastructure crumbing and streets in total disrepair.
LINK
Quite a challenge to drive down these streets. Pothole dodging has become an art.
V/O:
The Damplaas clients despair at the prospect of this municipality being tasked to take over from Damplaas.
Jannie:
As ek vat hoe werk hulle op die oomblik by die munisipaliteit wat so onbetroubaar is. Ek kan nie dink hoe ons gaan oorleef nie, hoe ons konstante krag gaan kry nie. Die ouens in die dorp het nie eens konstante krag nie, hoe gaan hulle dit vir ons op die please voorsien? Dis vir my ‘n saak van onmoontlikheid dat dit kan gebeur. Ek kan glad nie sien hoe dit kan werk nie.
V/O:
Damplaas customers can’t understand the court action. Having always done things by the book, they say – they have a current contract with Eskom, and they have been licensed by the National Energy Regulator to distribute power in that particular area. It seems that SALGA now wants to nullify these long-standing legal agreements.

It’s no wonder then, that SALGA’s sudden interest has raised some serious questions:
Derek:
Like why this High Court action and why now, why would they want to outlaw and agreement with the National Energy Regulator that has been around for 4 decades, and why they would want to hand over a successful electricity distribution service to a municipality that is dysfunctional?
V/O:
We hoped SALGA would provide the answers, but they declined to participate in our story saying, since the matter is before courts, they can’t talk to the media.

So, with court documents as difficult to navigate as the potholes in Petrus Steyn, we turned to Dr Kagiso Pooe, a local government expert at the Wits School of Governance. He says SALGA has more than just Damplaas in its sights.
TK:
So, in this court application by SALGA there are about 9 respondents and some of them which most people would know would be Eskom, Sasol, some farming communities in this application that was sent to the high court.
V/O
All of these entities, big and small have been distributing electricity independently of municipalities for many years.

SALGA now wants this to stop and is basing its argument on two stipulations in the Constitution. First, that municipalities are responsible for electricity distribution within their jurisdictions.

And second, that they operate within a current system known as wall to wall local government.
TK:
Wall to wall simply means that every inch and square metre of South Africa must have a municipality. Before 1994 this was not the case.
V/O:
In the past, municipalities had boundaries and only supplied electricity within these boundaries. Outside these boundaries, Eskom not only distributed electricity to millions of individual clients but also supplied it in bulk to entities that created their own power grids, like SANPARKS, SASOL and, you guessed it, Damplaas.

In 1980, neither Eskom nor the municipality of Petrus Steyn distributed electricity to farms in the district, but there was a dire need for it.
V/O:
So, the entered into a contract with Eskom to buy electricity in bulk, and erected a network of powerlines to distribute the power. The agreement with Eskom is still in place.
LINK:
This is the main powerline from Eskom to the Petrus Steyn substation. Here there are two transformers, one feeding power to the town, the other to Damplaas clients.
V/O:
The Damplaas network is 25% cheaper than Eskom’s rural tariffs and supplies a significant number of farms and farming industries with electricity. Jan Snyman is the Chair of the Board.

TK
As of December the former mayor and the CFO were arrested because of corruption. That’s jus the first thing. The Auditor general has long raised, for the last three years has raised the fact that they have not really been accountable with their finances and what they do. So by all intents and purposes it is a collapsed municipality and the region is a collapsing region.
V/O
And if this municipality is unable supply power to the district, it will have disastrous consequences for farmers.
Derek:
Could you farm without Damplaas electricity?

Thabu:
It won’t be possible to farm without Damplaas. If I do not have electricity, I must stop popato farming. And what is going to happen to the people that is working for me? All the potato farmers make us of lots and lots of people working for them.
V/O:
The SALGA court action implies that the local Nketoana Municipality in Petrus Steyn will have to recreate this extensive network and run it. This for a municipality that currently owes Eskom two hundred and twenty million rand. So, if it’s not practical, what else could be at stake?

TK:
It is a simple answer this one. I will be quite shot. It is money. If you read what the auditor general says and what most government reports say, most, they probably talking about 80% of municipalities have financial problems. They are not able to raise revemue or there is not sysmes in place. So Salga is basicall seeing an opportunity to get some leve of revenue into these municipalities. That is the basica. It’s the money. It’s the money.
V/O:
And it is really big money. Between Eksom and the other power distributors, sixty billion rand is collected from non-municipal clients every year. It seems SALGA want municipalities to access these funds.

Given their track record in delivering services, it’s baffling as to why municipalities would take on the additional burden of delivering electricity. But the Damplaas users say the municipalities themselves didn’t ask SALGA to approach the courts.
TK
If you are failing at doing just the basics of what you’re supposed to be doing, how then do you expect them now to get into something as complex as energy reticulation, being able to collect monies. Currently, no. South African municipalities are not in a position to be able to do this.
V/O:
SALGA, though, remains adamant that what it is asking is within the law.
TK:
No, no, they are not wrong, they are hanging onto something that is in black and white. But if you do this, you are hamstringing individuals who are …. I think some people do a good job in local government... but you are hamstringing them with an additional thing that they will jot be able to do, and it would be unfair to put these local governments in that position.
V/O:
So, it seems that Damplaas has been caught in the crossfire of a SALGA bid to get municipalities access to billions of rand in electricity. They have vowed to fight the application tooth and nail together with the other respondents. And because the motion hinges on constitutional mandates, the case is likely to end up in our apex court.

And while a protracted legal battle looms, Damplaas clients like the Wepners continue making the most of reliable electricity. Whether future generations do the same, remains to be seen.

Currently, no. South African municipalities are not in a position to be able to do this. V/O: SALGA, though, remains adamant that what it is asking is within the law. TK: No, no, they are not wrong, they are hanging onto something that is in black and white. But if you do this, you are hamstringing individuals who are …. I think some people do a good job in local government... but you are hamstringing them with an additional thing that they will jot be able to do, and it would be unfair to put these local governments in that position. V/O: So, it seems that Damplaas has been caught in the crossfire of a SALGA bid to get municipalities access to billions of rand in electricity. They have vowed to fight the application tooth and nail together with the other respondents. And because the motion hinges on constitutional mandates, the case is likely to end up in our apex court. And while a protracted legal battle looms, Damplaas clients like the Wepners continue making the most of reliable electricity. Whether future generations do the same, remains to be seen.

metadata.Further information: Damplaas Kragbron In a time where South Africa’s energy supply is in serious trouble, with rolling blackouts and near unaffordable power tariffs, new solutions are needed. And there is an example of a private solution that has been working exceptionally well for 30 years – but it is now also under serious threat. Damplaas Kragbron has been supplying reliable and affordable electricity to their community for more than 30 years. They have 320 km of power lines and has 175 transformers and supply power to the districts of Heilron, Lindely, Bethlehem and Reitz. It is situated in the Freestate town of Petrus Steyn. It has been highly successful and is well maintained. They buy electricity in bulk from Eskom and distribute it via their network with a small additional fee added. It all started 40 years ago when Eskom was not yet supplying power in the area. The farmers stood together and decided to establish their own network to get electricity to the various farms in the various districts and over the years it has grown to a network spanning 320 km. The network is crucial to the many irrigation farmers, chicken farms and other users such as a fertilizer factory and maize silos. The network supplies power to these enities and farmer who would not otherwise have had access to power. And their tariffs are 13% cheaper than Eskom’s rural tariffs and 20% cheaper than the local Neketoane municipality in Reitz. The whole network is currently valued at more than R50 million and was built with private money. They also have an additional 25 transformers which Eskom continuously want to borrow. They maintain the infrastructure and when Eskom customers lose power, they are still online. Truly a success story!! But that is not the end of it. Last week they were served with papers in which SALGA demands that the network be transferred to the dysfunctional and bankrupt local municipality. SALGA’s argument is that only municipalities are allowed to distribute electricity. Damplaas is opposing this, because if this is allowed to happen not only will tariffs skyrocket when the municipality takes over, the municipality does not have the capacity or knowledge to maintain the network. It all spells disaster for something that is working so well, and it will jeopardise farming operations in numerous districts, with severe job losses. Instead of trying to bring a perfectly functioning project into a failing system, why not learn from it and rather duplicate it in other places, the farmers ask. Interviewees: Jan Snyman -- MD of Damplaas Kragbron Thabu Bosman -- Damplaas lawyer and potato farmer SALGA TK Pooe, Wits School of Governance Case studies: • Johan Claassen who has 42 000 chickens and for whom power is crucial • Jannie Wepner an irrigation farmer, farming with maize.
